title: Asking for the working
objectives: Ask for step-by-step working, check each step, and tell when a chatbot is the wrong tool for the job.

screens.prose: Two replies to the same question give the same final figure. Both are invented examples.

lines: You: A share costs £50. It rises 20%, then falls 20%. What is it worth now?
params.title: Reply A (an invented example)

lines: You: A share costs £50. It rises 20%, then falls 20%. What is it worth now?
Step 2: after the rise it is £60.
Step 4: after the fall it is £48.
params.title: Reply B (an invented example)

screens.question: Tap the reply you can check without redoing the whole sum yourself.

hints.text: Which reply shows how it got £48?
One reply has four steps.
Reply B shows each step, so you can check each one quickly.

feedback.correct: Reply B shows four steps, each small enough to check at a glance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the reply that shows how it got there.

byKey.left: Reply A gives only £48. To check it you must redo the whole sum; there is nothing to follow.

explain.text: Both say £48, and £48 is right. But only Reply B lets you see why: each step is a small sum you can check in seconds. That is why you ask for the working.

screens.prose: Ask for the **working step by step**, then **check each step**, not only the answer. Here is a worked reply to a new question.

lines: You: A coat costs £80. It is cut by 25% in a sale, then the sale price rises by 25%. What does it cost now? Show your working.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Tap the step that goes wrong.

hints.text: In step 3, 25% of what is taken?
The rise is on the sale price, not the original.
Step 3 should be 25% of £60, which is £15, giving a final £75.

feedback.correct: Step 3 takes 25% of £80, but the rise is on the sale price, £60. It should be £15, and the final price £75.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what each percentage is taken of.

byKey.l5: Step 4 follows from step 3. The slip is earlier: step 3 used the wrong base.

explain.text: Step 3 takes 25% of £80 instead of the sale price, £60. The right steps give 25% of £60 = £15 and a final price of £75, not £80. The final £80 looks neat, which is how a wrong step hides behind a right-looking total.

screens.prose: A chatbot turns 1% a month into a yearly rate: "1% a month for 12 months is 12 × 1% = 12% a year." Each month's 1% is on a balance that has already grown.

lines: Step 1: the rate is 1% a month.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What is the true yearly rate, compounding monthly? Give a percentage to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: What do you multiply by each month?
Twelve months multiply by $1.01^{12}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.01 twelve times, then take off the 1.

byKey.added: That is step 3's 12%: it added the months. Each 1% is on a grown balance, so multiply.
byKey.factor: That is $1.01^{12}$ itself. Take off 1 to get the rate: 12.68%.

explain.text: Monthly growth multiplies: $1.01^{12} \approx 1.1268$. So the yearly rate is 12.68%, and step 3's addition was the slip. The steps let you find exactly where.

screens.prose: A chatbot is a good tool for some jobs and the wrong tool for others. Think about what it does: it writes likely text.

rows: today's facts, exact sums you cannot check, deciding for you

screens.question: Select all that apply: which are good jobs for a chatbot?

options.text: Drafting a polite email to a client
Explaining what a bond yield is
Brainstorming names for a new fund
Telling you a share's price right now
options.why: A model's text was gathered at an earlier date; without live data, a price now is invented.

options.text: Deciding which fund you should buy
options.why: A decision with your money needs your judgement and your checks, not likely text.

options.text: Adding 300 trade amounts you will not check
options.why: An exact sum you will not check is where a slip does the most harm. Use a spreadsheet.

hints.text: Which jobs need fresh facts or exact sums?
Read the right-hand column.
Drafting, explaining and brainstorming suit it. A live price, a decision for you and an unchecked sum do not.

feedback.correct: Drafting, explaining and brainstorming: work you can read and judge yourself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which jobs need fresh facts, exact sums or your own decision.

explain.text: A chatbot is good where a likely, well-written answer is what you want and you can judge it: drafts, explanations, ideas. It is the wrong tool where only a fresh fact, an exact sum or your own decision will do.

screens.prose: A colleague says of a reply: "It showed its working, so it must be right." The working below is an invented example.

lines: Working: 25% of £80 is £20, so the sale price is £60. 25% of £60 is £15. £60 + £15 = £75.
Working: 25% of £80 is £20, so the sale price is £60. 25% of £80 is £20. £60 + £20 = £80.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What is wrong with "it showed its working, so it is right"?

options.text: Working can be wrong too, and can be written to fit an answer given first; check each step
Nothing: a model that shows its working has worked the answer out properly
options.why: You took the working as proof. The second working shows a wrong step leading to a wrong answer.

options.text: Shown working is always made up, so it should be ignored completely
options.why: Working is often right, as in the first reply. It is useful because you can check it.

options.text: Only long working is reliable; short working should not be trusted at all
options.why: Length is not the test. Each step is.

hints.text: Look at the second working. Is each step right?
Its third sentence takes 25% of £80 again.
Working is text like any other. It helps because you can check it, not because it is there.

feedback.correct: Working is likely text too. It is useful because each step can be checked, not because it exists.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the second working.

byKey.shown-right: You took the working as proof. The second reply's working has a wrong step; and when the answer comes first, the working can be written to fit it.

explain.text: Working is written token by token, like the answer. When the answer comes first, the steps after it can be written to fit it, right or wrong. So working is a way to check, not a guarantee: check each step.

screens.prose: An auditor needs the exact total of 2,000 daily trade amounts from a file, to the penny.

rows: adds exactly what is in the cells

screens.question: Which tool should do the sum?

options.text: A spreadsheet, with a quick estimate to check it lands right
A chatbot, asked to show its working step by step
options.why: 2,000 steps of working is too long to check. An exact sum belongs in a spreadsheet.

options.text: A mental estimate alone
options.why: An estimate gives the rough size, not the total to the penny.

options.text: Two chatbots, comparing their totals
options.why: Two sets of likely text that agree are still not an exact sum.

hints.text: Which tool adds exactly what is in the cells?
Read the middle row.
A spreadsheet adds exactly; an estimate checks the result is the right size.

feedback.correct: A spreadsheet adds exactly; a rough estimate confirms the size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which tool is built to add exactly.

explain.text: For an exact sum of many numbers, a spreadsheet or a short script is simply the better tool. A rough estimate still checks it lands in the right place. A chatbot adds nothing here but risk.

screens.prose: Steps let you find the slip. Monthly growth compounds: $$1.01^{12} - 1 \approx 12.68\% \text{, not } 12 \times 1\% = 12\%$$ So ask for the working and check each step. Use a calculator or spreadsheet where only an exact sum will do.
screens.question: Which habit catches a wrong step that hides behind a neat total?

options.text: Checking each step of the working, not only the total
Checking only that the total looks neat
options.why: The coat's wrong £80 looked neat. Neat totals hide slips.

options.text: Trusting working that sounds confident
Asking for shorter working
options.why: Shorter working hides more, not less.

feedback.correct: Check each step: the slip is in a step, not in the look of the total.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall where the coat's slip was.

screens.prose: A desk rule says: any figure a chatbot produces is recomputed in the desk's own model before use. A chatbot turns a fee of 0.5% a month into "6% a year".

lines: Chatbot: 0.5% a month is 12 × 0.5% = 6% a year.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Recompute the yearly figure, compounding monthly. Give a percentage to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: What does the fee multiply by each month?
Twelve months multiply by $1.005^{12}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.005 twelve times, then take off the 1.

byKey.added: That is the chatbot's 6%: it added the months. Compounding gives a little more.

explain.text: Compounding twelve monthly charges of 0.5% gives $1.005^{12} - 1 \approx 0.0617$, so 6.17% a year. The gap looks small, but on a large fund it is real money. The desk rule exists so that small slips like this never reach a client.

ideas: Ask for the working step by step, then check each step: a wrong step can hide behind a right-looking total.
Working is likely text too, and can be written to fit an answer; it helps because you can check it, not because it is there.
Use a chatbot for drafts, explanations and ideas; use a calculator or spreadsheet for exact sums, and live sources for today's facts.

formula.name: Monthly to yearly
formula.note: 1% a month is 12.68% a year, not 12%.

summary.trap: "It showed its working, so it is right" is wrong. Check each step.

quiz.question: Why ask a chatbot to show its working?

options.text: So you can check each step and find any slip
Because working proves the answer is right
options.why: Working can be wrong too. Its value is that you can check it.

options.text: Because longer replies are more accurate
Because it is more polite
options.why: It is about checking, not manners.

feedback.correct: Steps can be checked one at a time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what you can do with steps that you cannot do with a bare answer.

explain.text: A bare answer can only be checked by redoing the whole problem. Steps let you check each small sum and find exactly where a slip happened.

quiz.question: Which job is a chatbot the wrong tool for?

options.text: Giving today's exchange rate with no live data
Drafting a meeting agenda
options.why: Drafting suits it: you can read and fix the draft.

options.text: Explaining what inflation means
options.why: Explaining suits it, and you can check the explanation.

options.text: Suggesting questions for an interview

feedback.correct: Today's rate came after its text was gathered.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a job that needs a fresh fact.

explain.text: Without live data a model cannot know today's rate, so any figure is invented. Drafting, explaining and brainstorming produce text you can judge yourself.

quiz.question: A price of £200 rises 10% and then falls 10%. A chatbot says it ends at £200. What does it end at?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The fall is taken on the risen price.

byKey.same: That is the chatbot's slip: it took the 10% fall on £200. The fall is on £220.
byKey.drop: That is the loss, £2. The question asks for the final price.

explain.text: The rise takes £200 to £220. The fall is 10% of £220, which is £22, so the price ends at £198, not £200. The chatbot's slip is a wrong base in one step.
